title: Oscar and the Choir
premise: Ada Eastwick, a mercenary whose god of oaths fell silent a generation ago, survives by guiding smugglers through the Thornfell mountains—until a starving boy arrives speaking the dead tongue of the Choir, the divine chorus the usurper's armies supposedly exterminated. The child, Oscar, is not a survivor but a vessel: the Choir's last voice, hidden in mortal flesh, and the usurper's inquisitors are already climbing the passes to cut it out of him. Ada must choose between the invisible life she built on the ruins of her faith and the dangerous truth that her god never died—only went quiet to hide Oscar. In the end, Ada smuggles Oscar not to safety but to the usurper's capital, where he sings before the assembled armies; the Choir's voice shatters the usurper's claim of divine sanction, and Ada pays the price of survival by surrendering her own silence, taking Oscar's secret into herself as the god's new vessel so the boy can live as a mortal child.
about_author: Juniper Crane is the pen name of a former mountain guide who traded trail maps for manuscript pages and never quite stopped listening for echoes in high passes. They write fantasy about people whose loyalties cost more than their lives.

chapters.title: The Silent Tithe
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada guides a smuggler caravan through Thornfell, paying her ritual tithe to a shrine of the god who no longer answers. Establishes her rules: no passengers, no questions, no names. Emotional beat: weary competence masking grief over a faith that abandoned her.

chapters.title: A Knock at the Warden's Door
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. A half-frozen boy arrives at Ada's remote warden station, speaking a language Ada recognizes only from her grandmother's heresy trials—the tongue of the Choir. She should turn him out. Emotional beat: instinct warring with a mercy she thought she'd buried.

chapters.title: What the Boy Said in His Sleep
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Oscar talks in a dead language while fevered, and the station's old oath-stones—silent for twenty years—hum in answer. Ada tests him deliberately and the stones glow. Emotional beat: dread curdling into awe.

chapters.title: Inquisitor Veyne Descends the Pass
chapters.summary: Veyne's POV. The usurper's chief inquisitor, hunting the 'last echo,' interrogates a mountain village and executes an old woman who once sang a forbidden hymn. He is patient, devout, and certain. Emotional beat: cold, institutional menace.

chapters.title: The Price of a Passenger
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada breaks her own rules and agrees to move Oscar, trading her smuggler contacts for safe passage papers. Her oldest friend, Bren, demands to know what she's carrying. Emotional beat: the first cost of the secret, paid in trust.

chapters.title: Hymns in the Dark
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, first time. Through Oscar's eyes we learn he doesn't fully know what he is—only that voices have lived inside him since the soldiers burned his village. The voices comfort him; they also frighten Ada. Emotional beat: innocence as an unbearable burden.

chapters.title: The Toll of Thornhollow Bridge
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. At a checkpoint, Veyne's agents inspect the caravan. Ada hides Oscar in a corpse-wagon, and the oath-stone sewn into his coat sings one clear note. An agent hears it. Emotional beat: near-catastrophe and Ada's cold-blooded nerve.

chapters.title: Bren's Betrayal
chapters.summary: Bren's POV. Pressured by debt and fear, Bren sells Ada's route to the inquisition—not knowing the cargo, only that it's worth gold. He tells himself it isn't betrayal. Emotional beat: the ordinary corruption of decent men.

chapters.title: The Shrine That Answered
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Sheltering in the ruined shrine, Ada prays out of habit and the god—through Oscar—answers for the first time in twenty years. Not with comfort: with a task. Emotional beat: rage at a god who returns only when it needs something.

chapters.title: What the Choir Was
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The voices show Oscar visions: the Choir were the god's many mouths, and the usurper slaughtered them to monopolize divine word. Oscar is the last mouth, smuggled out as an infant. Emotional beat: a child comprehending why everyone who loved him died.

chapters.title: The Free Cities Will Not Listen
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada reaches the free cities' council to warn them the usurper's armies are coming and that Oscar could rally the faithful. They see a heretic child and a disgraced mercenary. Emotional beat: the law's blindness; justice will not come from councils.

chapters.title: Veyne Closes the Net
chapters.summary: Veyne's POV. Veyne corners Ada in the lower city, offering a bargain: deliver the boy and be pardoned, restored, remembered. He speaks of the god with genuine love—and of Oscar as an abomination to be silenced. Emotional beat: temptation dressed as mercy.

chapters.title: The Rooftop Choir
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Hunted through the city, Oscar panics and the voices erupt—every bell in the district rings unstruck, and hundreds of citizens fall to their knees weeping. The free cities see the miracle; the usurper's spies see a weapon. Emotional beat: wonder that cannot stay hidden.

chapters.title: Ashes of the Smuggler's Road
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Veyne burns Ada's mountain routes, her contacts, her history of invisibility—everything she built to survive is now evidence. Bren, guilt-ridden, dies getting her the last maps out. Emotional beat: grief for the self she can never return to.

chapters.title: The Choice at the Crossroads
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada can run west with Oscar beyond the usurper's reach and let the war come to the free cities—or go east, into the capital, and put the boy in front of the armies. Oscar asks her not to decide for him. Emotional beat: Ada learning that protection is not the same as ownership.

chapters.title: Marching on the Capital
chapters.summary: Veyne's POV. The usurper's army advances; Veyne, unsettled by the bell miracle, begins privately doubting the official history of the Choir's extermination. He finds a suppressed archive that changes nothing—and everything. Emotional beat: a true believer's first crack.

chapters.title: The Long Walk to the Gates
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Ada walks Oscar up the pilgrim road to the capital gates under a false penitent's hood, past refugees and gallows. He is terrified and, for the first time, willing. Emotional beat: courage as a decision made while shaking.

chapters.title: Before the Iron Throne of Lies
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Captured and dragged before the usurper, Ada is offered the same bargain: renounce the boy. Instead she speaks the old tongue aloud—the first words of her testimony—buying Oscar the crowd's attention. Emotional beat: Ada spending her invisibility as deliberately as coin.

chapters.title: The Song That Unmade a Crown
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Oscar sings before the usurper, the army, and the city: the Choir's true voice, and with it the memory of every oath the usurper swore and broke. Soldiers kneel; the usurper's divine sanction dies in the square. Emotional beat: triumph inseparable from terror.

chapters.title: What Veyne Did With the Truth
chapters.summary: Veyne's POV. Ordered to execute Oscar, Veyne instead reads the suppressed archive aloud and turns his inquisitors' swords aside. He does not become a good man; he becomes an honest one, at the cost of everything. Emotional beat: justice arriving through a compromised instrument.

chapters.title: The Price Ada Paid
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. The Choir cannot survive in one mortal child; the god offers a vessel. Ada accepts—taking the voices into herself, surrendering her silence and her selfhood piece by piece—so Oscar can be only a boy. Emotional beat: the full weight of survival's price, paid willingly.

chapters.title: The Warden's Empty Station
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, epilogue. Years later, a grown Oscar returns to the mountain station, now tended by the free cities as a shrine. Ada lives within the stones, no longer quite Ada, and when he sings the old tongue, she answers. Emotional beat: mourning and peace in the same breath.
